title: ईशावास्य उपनिषद् — Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad
subtitle: Living in the World Without Being Possessed by It
summary: Eighteen mantras that close the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda: the shortest of the principal Upaniṣads, and one of the most argued over.
opening: What truly belongs to us? Can we live fully without becoming enslaved by possession? Can action and renunciation coexist? What is the Self that remains unchanged amid all change?
facts: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, adhyāya 40 — in the Kāṇva recension (Kāṇva Saṃhitā 40), the source of this text
18 (Kāṇva). The Mādhyandina recension’s VS 40 has 17, in another order
Mostly anuṣṭubh; 4 and 18 triṣṭubh; 8 and 16 irregular; 17 treated as prose (yajus)
Śaṅkara (Advaita), Vedānta Deśika (Viśiṣṭādvaita), Madhva (Dvaita), Mahīdhara (on VS 40)
objectives: Read the eighteen mantras in Sanskrit with a transliteration you can trust, and know what each word is doing.
Explain in your own words what the first mantra asks of a person, and why ‘renounce and enjoy’ is only one of its possible readings.
State how Śaṅkara, Vedānta Deśika and Madhva each understand ‘the Lord’ and ‘the Self’, and where they disagree.
Explain why vidyā and avidyā in mantras 9–11 are not simply ‘knowledge’ and ‘ignorance’.
Recognise the Vedic imagery of the final prayers and tell it apart from later symbolic readings.
Tell the ancient text from the modern voice explaining it, on any page.

key_questions.q: What is the world, and whose is it?
Should one act, or renounce action?
What happens to those who ‘slay the self’?
How can the same reality be still and swift, near and far?
What changes in a person who sees all beings in the self?
What is the Self like, considered in itself?
Why do both ‘avidyā’ and ‘vidyā’ lead into darkness — and how can both lead beyond death?
What does a person ask for at death?

reading_guide.title: Mantras 1–3: the vision and the choice
reading_guide.text: The Lord in all things; letting go; working without being stained; the fate of those who obscure the self.

reading_guide.title: Mantras 4–8: the Self
reading_guide.text: Paradox (4–5), vision (6–7) and description by negation (8). The centre of the Upaniṣad.

reading_guide.title: Mantras 9–14: two triads
reading_guide.text: The same pattern twice — two paths that each lead to darkness, a teaching received from the wise, and a combination that ‘crosses death’. The most disputed mantras.

reading_guide.title: Mantras 15–18: the prayers
reading_guide.text: The prayer of a dying person to the Sun, the breath, the mind and Agni. Shared with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (5.15.1); the last is a Ṛgveda verse.

sections.heading: The name and what it means
sections.label: linguistic
paras: Like many Vedic texts, the Upaniṣad is named after its opening words, īśā vāsyam, ‘to be dwelt in (or covered) by the Lord’. It is also called the Īśopaniṣad, ‘the Upaniṣad of the Lord’, and, from its place in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitopaniṣad. The name does not settle how its first words are divided: Madhva reads one compound, īśāvāsyam, ‘the dwelling of the Lord’ («ईशस्यावासयोग्यमीशावास्यम्»).

sections.heading: Why this short text matters
sections.label: traditional
paras: The Īśā is the only one of the principal Upaniṣads that is part of a Saṃhitā, the Veda’s collection of mantras, and it stands at the very end of it. The tradition takes that placement as meaningful: Śaṅkara begins by saying that these mantras, unlike those before them, are not used in ritual, because they reveal the Self, which no action produces or alters («कर्मस्वविनियुक्ताः»); Vedānta Deśika says the same in verse. It is traditionally placed first in the list of the ten principal Upaniṣads, and all three Vedānta schools compared here wrote commentaries on it.

In eighteen mantras it raises most of the questions the longer Upaniṣads explore at length: the relation of the Lord to the world, of action to knowledge, of the individual to the whole, and what a person can hope for at death.

sections.heading: A narrative introduction
sections.label: reflection
paras: The Upaniṣad opens without a story or a speaker. It begins with a claim about everything — all this, whatever moves in this moving world, is to be seen as dwelt in by the Lord — and turns at once to the listener: let go, and so enjoy; do not covet; whose is wealth? It then speaks to a person who must go on acting in the world, a hundred years of action that need not stain. It warns of worlds of blind darkness for those who obscure the self. Then it falls silent about the listener and describes, in paradox, what the self is: unmoving yet faster than thought, far and near, within all this and outside it. It promises that the one who sees all beings in the self will not shrink from anything, and asks what delusion or grief could remain for one who sees oneness.

Then the text does something unexpected. Twice it tells us that those who follow one way enter blind darkness, and those who follow its opposite enter a greater darkness; twice it says the wise taught that each way has its own result; twice it says that the one who knows both together crosses death and reaches immortality. The commentators have argued for a thousand years over what these pairs are. The Upaniṣad ends in prayer: a person at the end of life asks the Sun to draw back its golden lid so that the face of the real can be seen, recognises the person in the sun as himself, gives his breath back to the air and his body to the fire, and asks Agni to lead him by a good path.

The questions it asks — what belongs to us, how to act without being consumed by action, what in us does not change, what to ask for at the end — are not tied to any century. That is why so short a text has been read so closely for so long.

sections.heading: The principal themes
sections.label: direct
paras: The Lord in all things (1). Action without attachment (2). The consequences of ignorance of the self (3). The paradoxical nature of the Self (4–5). Seeing all beings in the self, and the end of fear, delusion and grief (6–7). The Self described by negation: bodiless, pure, untouched by evil (8). The relation of two kinds of practice, each incomplete alone (9–14). The prayers of the dying (15–18).

sections.heading: Recensions and variants
sections.label: linguistic
paras: The Śukla Yajurveda survives in two recensions, and the Upaniṣad in both. The Kāṇva text, followed here and by every commentary used, has eighteen mantras. The Mādhyandina text (VS 40) has seventeen: it puts the sambhūti mantras (12–14) before the vidyā mantras (9–11), reads ablatives in place of instrumentals in mantra 10, has ‘vi cikitsati’ for ‘vijugupsate’ in mantra 6 and ‘pretyāpi gacchanti’ for ‘pretyābhigacchanti’ in mantra 3, lacks the prayer to Pūṣan of 15b–16a, replaces the repeated line of 17 with ‘klibe smara’, and ends with ‘yo ’sāv āditye puruṣaḥ so ’sāv aham | om khaṃ brahma’. Within the Kāṇva tradition, too, readings differ: Mahīdhara and the Kāṇva Saṃhitā witness read arśat in mantra 4, the Upaniṣad witnesses arṣat. Every such difference is listed and classified on the Sources page.
